With a bachelor's degree in communication and 10 years of professional writing experience, his expertise is spread across a variety of different pop culture topics -- from TV series to books and the latest LEGO sets .

articles.title: Furious Is the Best New Show You’re Not Watching Yet
articles.summary: Hulu's eight-episode crime thriller’s first season starring Emmy Rossum and Lola Petticrew just wrapped up this week and its incredible finale locked in this show as my favorite new drama — and maybe TV show, period — of the year.
articles.body:
If you’re in need of a new show to binge over this (or any) long weekend, I’m imploring you: Watch Furious. The eight-episode crime thriller’s first season just wrapped up this week and its incredible finale locked in this show as my favorite new drama — and maybe TV show, period — of the year.

It’s already been a good year for TV show debuts. A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms had a built-in audience, being part of the Game of Thrones-verse, but stood out with its charming buddy duo in Dunk and Egg. Widow’s Bay grew into the breakout TV hit of early summer, with people fawning over its idiosyncratic genre blend and stellar ensemble. Lanterns is doing pretty well, too (when it’s not pissing some people off ). But Hulu’s Furious is the latest surprise show that has broken containment, growing week-over-week — the finale had 90% more views than the premiere, which already cracked the bottom of Nielson’s streaming charts, according to Variety . It’s already been greenlit for a second season . Basically, Furious is special and people are noticing.

Created by Elizabeth Meriweather, who’s best known for New Girl, Furious is just barely based on the 1987 movie Black Widows, which starred Debra Winger and Theresa Russell, but toss aside any assumptions you might make based on that creative pedigree combo. It’s hardly a breezy half-hour sitcom, though it knows how to deploy humor to cut through the bleakness, and has almost nothing in common with the ‘80s film aside from the women serial killer/Fed dynamic.

Furious is often a difficult watch based on the details of its dead-serious subject matter, but it has an almost unbelievable iron grip over its pacing and tone. Things will happen that make your stomach churn, but it never crosses over into exploitation, handling all of the show’s many thorny complexities head-on with care. The mounting tension is so dialed in that scenes — sometimes action-driven, other times just an interrogation — feel palpably dangerous, creating that propulsive “I gotta watch another episode” itch. Frankly, I’m envious of those starting it now, when you don’t have to wait a week between episodes. (At the same time, I’m also relieved it got the old-school weekly episode release treatment to find an audience and wasn’t dumped all at once.)

On paper, Furious may sound like any other decent cat-and-mouse crime drama, but it really is so much more. That’s in no small part thanks to the depth of characters and electric performances, especially from its core cast of women characters, all (as the title implies) of whom are full of justified rage. Petticrew — who was also great in Say Nothing, last year’s excellent Hulu series about the Irish Republican Army during The Troubles — gives Catherine a trauma-laden, erratic unpredictability with huge emotional peaks and valleys, and yet never becomes hammy. Rossum — probably best known for Shameless and Phantom of the Opera — simmers as Alice, who can be stoic, cruel, selfish, and compassionate all at once. Perhaps best of all is Quincy Tyler Bernstine — while lauded for stage acting, she’s made plenty of prestige-y TV appearances — as Nora Washington, Alice’s boss and Greek mythology enthusiast who doesn’t waste a single word during her screen time. The men are pretty good, too: Scoot McNairy as the exhausted good cop, Jake Lacy as the insatiable bad cop, Rob Yang as a sort-of-stupid FBI agent, Danny McCarthy as a corrupt jerk FBI ASAC, and Steve Way as the hopelessly romantic and mold-breaking comic relief .

I’m being purposefully cagey about the grimier plot specifics because I really think new watchers are best served in knowing as little as possible before going in, learning the dark, reality-coded secrets of Furious as you watch. But if you want to take a dive into a messed-up series that will almost definitely be in Emmy conversations next year, you know where to look.

Leanne Butkovic (she/they) is an Editorial Programming Manager at IGN, where they've also written about TV, movies, and games.

articles.title: Metal Gear Solid Master Collection Vol. 2 Review, Gameplay Impressions, Videos and Top Features
articles.summary: Metal Gear Solid Master Collection Vol. 2 from developer Konami brings modern beloved entries of the historic series to the forefront of gaming once more.
articles.body:
Metal Gear Solid Master Collection Vol. 2 from developer Konami brings modern beloved entries of the historic series to the forefront of gaming once more.

The Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection from 2023 got the ball rolling with a generation of stealth classics with the perplexing, memorable overall narrative found early in the series.

Fast forward to now, Master Collection Vol. 2 brings 2008's Metal Gear Solid 4: Guns of the Patriots and 2010's Metal Gear Solid: Peace Walker to the limelight, finally freeing the former from its PlayStation 3 prison and latter from the handheld PSP once again.

Chicken equity? This may be the wildest jersey number trade yet

Guns of the Patriots finally being accessible on modern hardware would be merit enough to demand returning and new players alike grab Vol. 2. Tacking on the extra goodies and modern trappings just makes it all the better.

At the time of release, MGS4 was nearly unmatched in terms of visuals and overall immersion during moment-to-moment gameplay. The jarring sound design and stellar graphics did heavy lifting. Obviously, those things have aged since the PS3 era, to say the least.

Even so, 4K does MGS4 some serious justice. Everyone knew it looked good back then, but seeing it souped up in 2026 and holding its own despite being a PS3 title is…pretty impressive.

As most could have probably predicted, the gameplay holds up even better than the presentation.

At the time, Guns of the Patriots was a major shift for Metal Gear Solid. It left the comfortable confines of the past and decided to start being a standard-bearer instead, putting players in control of an AAA action experience.

In current times, the over-the-shoulder camera still feels modern, as does the ability to change things to first-person.

The stealth itself and active camo system is still one of the best in gaming, ever. It holds up rather surprisingly well, in part because the stealth genre, Splinter Cell included, sort of imploded over the last decade or so.

But much of it is simply because it was so good , even back then. The sheer number of ways to approach a situation, funny enemy AI and punchiness of it all meshed perfectly with the ambiance and story.

Then there's Peace Walker, the game that first really leaned into the base-building aspects of later entries. Its shocking number of missions and the quick-hitting format of those went on to influence plenty, including much of what people see in mobile games these days.

That's a compliment, by the way. Few mobile games come close. Peace Walker is a blast in near-2027, even if the almost-intimidating number of missions starts to get a little repetitive.

There isn't much all that different with these classics here. Stellar gameplay, both for powerful consoles or handhelds of the era, still holds up well and is a blast, hence the classical nature of both in the first place.

This is Metal Gear Solid. Don't expect to enter Guns of the Patriots understanding much of anything. That even goes for those who have played it in the past.

Kidding aside, it's still gripping and memorable. And if we're talking about story beats like say, algorithms influencing things and privatization, etc., it sure feels right at home in modern times.

The five acts in Guns of the Patriots remain refreshingly diverse in locale and execution, be it slinking through a battleship or sneaking around various bits of nature.

It's a narrative feast of unique goofiness to this day, with the boogeyman "nanomachines" explaining away anything that might not make a lick of sense. Snake wants to off Liquid Ocelot, is the tried-and-true basic premise, with lots of unforgettable, weird boss battles and stuff standing in his way.

Peace Walker's tale, on the other hand, is decidedly more, well, handheld. There are some comicbook-like trappings and memorable stuff going on, but the difference is obvious. Again, not a bad thing. For some, it'll harken back to some nostalgia bits of handheld glory days.

Master Collection Vol. 2 runs well, as expected, but it makes some head-scratching decisions, too. There are multiple launchers for the game on PC, which is a little odd. There's a separate launcher for bonus features, for example.

Even so, the sheer amount of content here is a bit staggering. There's a little Game Boy title tucked into here as well, plus the yawning expanse of what is essentially a Metal Gear Wikipedia included for good measure.

Guns of the Patriots is the real treat here for technical reasons and for the sheer fact it's an all-time classic that happens to, sort of wrap up the overall story and end the Hideo Kojima era.

That's not meant to sell Peace Walker short because it deserves its flowers for evolving not just the mobile game space, but future entries like MGS5 heavily took from it, too.

Taken as a whole, though, Guns of the Patriots is the far bigger deal here. And taking into account the extra stuff, sheer runtime and overall importance, one could argue this is far, far more important than the first Master Collection release.

No complaints, though, regardless. As the most important entry in this resurgence of Metal Gear Solid, this has been a long, long time coming and it's one of the few packages to truly be worth the wait.

articles.title: Nvidia will officially bring DLSS 5 to older GPUs — but won’t give gamers full control
articles.summary: Nvidia will bring DLSS 5 to RTX 40, but won’t confirm that previously announced DLSS 5 games will still ship with the tech.
articles.body: Officially, Nvidia’s controversial DLSS 5 AI rendering was supposed to launch this evening with only a single game, only on Nvidia’s latest RTX 50 GPUs, and with developers in full control of their artistic vision. But unofficially, modders have already ported a leaked version of DLSS 5 to run on just about anything while cranking sliders to the max. Now, Nvidia is changing its plans. DLSS 5 is still launching first on RTX 50 GPUs, but it’s officially coming to older RTX 40-series GPUs as well, Nvidia spokesperson Rajal Maharaj confirms to The Verge. “Our current focus is on optimizing performance for the GeForce RTX 50 Series with model updates expected later this fall. Once RTX 50 Series performance is more fully tuned, we plan to work on expanding official support to the GeForce RTX 40 Series,” reads part of Nvidia’s statement. What about earlier RTX 30 and RTX 20-series GPUs, which modders successfully targeted as well, assuming you count “not exactly playable framerate and plenty of crashes” as successful? “Right now the focus is of course on 50-series,” Maharaj tells me. “Once we feel like the 50-series is in a good place, we’re going to look at the 40-series.” Now that the cat’s out of the bag, will gamers get full control over DLSS 5’s sliders the way modders already do? Nvidia says no: “For gamers, DLSS 5 is a simple on-or-off toggle,” the company confirms. “The more granular artistic controls are for developers, including model selection, Structure Intensity, Tone Intensity, automatic masking and custom per-pixel masking.” That said, the company tells me that developers could pass along certain controls in their own settings menus, like they’ve done with other graphics tech. (Early DLSS Super Resolution was also just an on/off toggle, but today’s games let you pick between varying levels of quality or even an exact percentage, depending on the game.) Assuming you don’t mind DLSS 5, one of the benefits is that it’s easy to integrate. Developers don’t need to tell DLSS 5 which objects are “silverware” and which are “furniture” because the AI models can automatically recognize and isolate objects in a scene, distinguishing between faces, textiles, foliage, and more to apply different amounts of AI processing. Game engines that already know which video game objects are which can help DLSS 5, too: > For more targeted control, semantic AI masking can automatically recognize scene objects, while engine-level masking allows artists to isolate specific props or groups of assets, such as glassware, water droplets or foliage, and apply custom neural lighting adjustments to those elements. Unreal Engine 5 has a native plugin, and Nvidia also has SDKs. Nvidia says developers can apply DLSS 5 to their entire game this way, or do it differently for different scenes, cutscenes, or portions of gameplay, and the company tells The Verge that its DLSS 5 models run on every single frame, so there’s no minimum framerate for it to work. We’re still waiting to find out if the early backlash against DLSS 5 scared away publishers and developers that had originally committed to the technology. Nvidia’s response to us today suggests that perhaps some companies have backed away. When we asked if the company could re-confirm that it will come to Assassin’s Creed Shadows, Hogwarts Legacy, Starfield, Resident Evil Requiem, and the other 12 originally-announced titles, this was the company’s only reply: “More games are on the way. Many developers are actively integrating DLSS 5, and we’ll share updates on upcoming titles as partners finalize their integrations.”

Polyphony Digital has revealed Gran Turismo 7’s next major update will mark the return of Autumn Ring , and includes a dozen new cars, the series debut of real-life circuit Sportsland Sugo, and a variety of other features.

The ‘Spec IV’ update will be delivered in two parts before the end of 2026; the first will arrive in October and the second will be available in December.

The first chunk of Spec IV will come with Sportland Sugo (a real-life race circuit located in Japan’s Miyagi Prefecture that currently hosts Super GT and Super Formula rounds) plus six new cars, a new ‘Vintage’ section featuring cars not available to purchase in GT as new, a ‘Car Concierge’ function players can use to order used and Legend cars, new driving challenges, a new car viewer, and a Collector Level cap increase.

The second half of Spec IV will include Autumn Ring, another six new cars, a new ‘Family’ mode for inexperienced players, a luck-based race with random cars called ‘Shuffle Race’, online drift trials, and a new difficulty level in the Power Pack.

Autumn Ring, first seen in the original Gran Turismo, was last included in 2013’s Gran Turismo 6. The GT7 version of Autumn Ring will include the original layout, and a new “greatly expanded layout.”

Highlights from the showcase included an extended look at Square Enix’s Final Fantasy VII Revelation, a clip from Zach Cregger’s upcoming Resident Evil movie, and the reveal of two new limited-edition DualSense controllers inspired by GTA 6 , but it was a presentation that was otherwise dominated by continued fan demands for Destiny 3 .

articles.title: Amid Concern in Japan, Dragon Ball Producer Toei Animation Denies Involvement in Saudi-France Paris Theme Park
articles.summary: Last week, France and Saudi Arabia made the surprise announcement that the Paris region of France will be getting a Dragon Ball theme park. This sparked varied reactions across the internet, with many comments in Japanese expressing concern regarding licensing rights and the lack of Japanese representation. This week, Dragon Ball anime producer Toei Animation released an official announcement denying involvement in the project. So what is happening with this proposed Dragon Ball theme park in France?
articles.body:
Last week, France and Saudi Arabia made the surprise announcement that the Paris region of France will be getting a Dragon Ball theme park . This sparked varied reactions across the internet, with many comments in Japanese expressing concern regarding licensing rights and the lack of Japanese representation. This week, Dragon Ball anime producer Toei Animation released an official announcement denying involvement in the project. So what is happening with this proposed Dragon Ball theme park in France?

In case you missed it, Saudi Arabia’s de facto ruler Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman made a two-day state visit to France last month, attending the closing ceremony of the Esports World Cup in Paris alongside French president Emmanuel Macron (source: Arab News ). This trip culminated in the surprise announcement of a new theme park project just outside Paris.

Posting on X in French on August 25, Macron said: “With Saudi Arabia, we are making an unprecedented announcement.” The French president went on to describe the proposal as three theme parks located in Cergy-Pontoise, northwest of Paris. He cited the 6 billion euro investment and predicted 22,000 jobs created by the project as something that hadn’t been seen “since Disneyland Paris.” It will be a “new global destination — here, in France.”

In the post, Macron mentioned his personal liking of Japanese comics (“You know of my interest in manga”), however he did not directly state what themes these three parks would have. However, a later official press release by the Île-de-France region on August 31 referred directly to one of the three being “a Dragon Ball park.”

News outlets worldwide, including Japanese ones like Mainichi Shimbun , swiftly picked up the story of a Dragon Ball theme park in France. However, this sparked backlash among some Japanese language commenters amid concerns that there was no visible Japanese representation or official announcement from license holders at the time.

Since then, Toei Animation, the studio behind the Dragon Ball anime, issued a statement regarding the park proposal, denying any prior knowledge or involvement.

“Recently, some media reports have suggested that ‘the decision has been made to build a Dragon Ball theme park in France,’ however our company (...) and relevant rights-holding companies have not granted any licences in relation to this matter, and we are not aware of any such plans,” stated Toei Animation.

Toei Animation is involved in the ongoing plan to build a Dragon Ball theme park in the Saudi Arabian capital of Riyadh, in a strategic partnership with Qiddiya Investment Company. In this case, Toei Animation directly announced the project on its website back in 2024, alongside concept images, a video and details of the project.

Dragon Ball Z Theme Park Concept Art (2024)

However, in its recent statement, Toei clarified that the concept images used by some news reports of a Paris park actually relate to the planned Dragon Ball theme park in Riyadh, and not to any France-based project. Although new Dragon Ball projects were announced at the 40th anniversary event in April, the rights to the franchise are complicated and involve several companies. Until further official announcements are made, it’s unclear if and when a France-based theme park featuring the late Akira Toriyama’s creations will become a reality. No opening date has been set, and construction is expected to take several ​years.

Saudi Arabia’s Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman is an open fan of video games and anime, making increasing investments in game companies through his MiSK foundation and its subsidiaries. Through related companies, he owns King of Fighters developer SNK, plus a 10% stake in Capcom , among others. The Qiddiya Investment Company, which is involved in the Dragon Ball Riyadh theme park, is owned by the Saudi Arabian sovereign wealth fund, the Public Investment Fund (PIF), of which the crown prince is chairman. On August 4, an investor group composed of PIF, Silver Lake and Affinity Partners completed a $55 billion leveraged buyout of video game giant EA .

Verity Townsend is a Japan-based freelance writer who previously served as editor, contributor and translator for the game news site Automaton West. She has also written about Japanese culture and movies for various publications.

articles.title: Marvel Secretly Developing New Live-Action Disney+ Project, Potentially Young Avengers or New Mutants
articles.summary: A flurry of reports point to Marvel secretly mounting a new live-action Disney+ series, potentially featuring characters from the Young Avengers or New Mutants.
articles.body:
A flurry of reports point to Marvel secretly mounting a new live-action Disney+ series, potentially featuring characters from the Young Avengers or New Mutants.

Last month, Murphy's Multiverse spotted that a fresh Marvel production company, Veil Productions, had been set up for a TV project. Now, there's also word on its production codename: "Slumber Party."

Marvel typically sets up a production company for each of its major projects, and these can be named something referencing the project itself. (Marvel's recent "Throttle Productions" is believed to be the team behind Ryan Gosling's upcoming Ghost Rider, for example.) So too with its production codenames, though these can also be deliberately obtuse.

The Most Surprising Avengers and Marvel Characters Not Announced for Doomsday

So, what could Veil refer to? In the Marvel comics, Veil was a young member of the Avengers Academy, and Slumber Party certainly points to a youthful setting. It's also the title of New Mutants #21, which introduced Warlock.

Marvel has been considering a standalone Young Avengers project for years, it is widely understood, with teases in several other MCU projects and an array of characters it could now include. Iman Vellani's excellent Ms. Marvel was last seen trying to form a team with Hailee Steinfeld's Kate Bishop, with Kathryn Newton's Cassie Lang also in their sights to recruit.

Beyond these, it's been years now since we checked in with Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness's America Chavez and The Falcon and the Winter Soldier's Patriot. There's also Ironheart's Riri Williams, plus Agatha and Vision Quest's Maximoff twins. Even Hulk has a son now, too.

When might we hear more? Marvel will hold a dedicated "Up Next From Marvel Television and Marvel Animation" panel at New York Comic-Con on October 8, which seems like a great time to make some form of announcement. Expect more detail on Vision Quest and Daredevil: Born Again Season 3 at the same time.

Every Confirmed Mutant in the MCU (So Far)

Any new Disney+ live-action series confirmation would be notable at this point, following the noticable slowdown in new Marvel (and Star Wars) live-action series getting the greenlight. After years of pumping out projects that left fans feeling like the studio was focused on quantity rather than quality (Secret Invasion, looking at you), Disney appears to have reigned in its balance sheet, while Marvel looks to be applying more quality control.

The timing for a Young Avengers project would also seem to make sense, perhaps focusing on the characters during or directly preceding the events of Avengers: Doomsday, making for a intriguing setup to Avengers: Secret Wars.

Earlier this week, it was reported that Noah Jupe had joined the cast of Avengers: Secret Wars in a hush-hush role that fans already believed they have sussed out.

articles.title: PUBG: DED.NET Developer Argues Making a Game for the Mass Market Where 'Nobody's Too Offended and Everybody Kind of Likes It' Has Become 'Box Office Poison'
articles.summary: PUBG: DED.NET developer Dave Curd has argued that making a video game for the mass market where "nobody's too offended and everybody kind of likes it" has become "box office poison."
articles.body:
PUBG — the battle royale that popularized the genre — already has a number of spinoffs. But none is as love it or hate it as DED.NET .

Like PUBG, DED.NET is a multiplayer first-person shooter that revolves around outlasting your enemies, but there are a number of key differences. Chief among them is roguelite progression that persists across runs, and a heavy-handed 1990s aesthetic dubbed “Grunge House.” But there’s more. Matches — even if you make it to the end — will come in at around the 25-30 minute mark, which makes it a digestible experience relative to PUBG’s more intense, longer-lasting battle royale. And while PUBG is available on console, DED.NET is built from the ground up for consoles.

Set in Cascadia in 1996, a world inspired by the Pacific Northwest of the 1990s, and with a reimagining of the PUBG formula beyond battle royale, DED.NET may prove divisive. That, creative director Dave Curd told IGN at gamescom, isn’t just okay — it’s exactly what the developers at Krafton want. In fact, Curd argued that making a game for everyone has become “box office poison.”

“Definitely PUBG was the one that brought the genre to prominence and then everyone was like, ‘What's my take? Is it destruction? Is it competitive play? Is it Twitch reactions?’ And you're picturing the games as I'm describing them,” Curd began.

“And ours is the rogue. This is the rogue version where you're always chasing a build, getting into hilarious shithousery along the way. You're telling hysterical stories, you're engaging in a world filled with Twin Peaks, X-Files, David Kronenberg, body horror. We're trying to make a real evocative, love it or hate it experience.

“I think the age of making something for the mass market... which, what is that anymore? I don't think that's safe. I don't think that's smart. I think making something that can really get a fandom, something where people feel seen and they connect with, and have just as many detractors, I think that's wiser than kind of, ‘Well, let's make sure nobody's too offended and everybody kind of likes it.’ So we're trying to be sexy, evocative, gory.”

Curd said the inspiration for DED.NET ’s Grunge House aesthetic includes grunge band Nirvana, Italian zombie movies, Grindhouse, and Tarantino movies. And, he believes that if DED.NET proves “sticky,” he expects other battle royale developers to give the ‘rogue multi-match journey’ mechanic a try.

“But what they won't be able to do is replicate our world where you can chop your hands off and replace them with machetes and have a standoff in a cult mansion, underground cellar filled with bodies,” he insisted. “We're just trying to serve up something fresh for the kids.”

What Curd is desperate to avoid here is apathy. He wants DED.NET to provoke a reaction, whether that’s good or bad. If it’s good, then great. If it’s bad, well Curd can work to turn that feeling around. But apathy is a death sentence for any video game’s prospects.

“I think middle of the road is box office poison,” Curd said. “You want lovers and haters. Haters care enough to hate, which means maybe you can reach them one day. Maybe a lot of people will see this and naturally say, ‘Hey, I don't want a Ford Bronco. I want a Ford Mustang. Keep fixing the Ford Mustang.’ And that's a very valid point. And my job is not to convince you to like cheese if you're not a cheese guy. But I think there's a lot of guys that will try it and say, ‘Okay, I'm pleasantly surprised. I'm in. They're taking a swing.’

“I've always said audiences will forgive anything but being bored. I think even if they hate us, they may respect us for taking a big swing, especially when a lot of the other big players circle their wagons, they focus on one mega product. PUBG and Krafton are out here trying to serve the fans and take big swings and try new stuff.”

Curd isn't alone in making this argument. Arrowhead, the developer of smash hit co-op shooter Helldivers 2, have long argued much the same. Indeed, Arrowhead's studio tagline is, "A game for everyone is a game for no one." This, Arrowhead has said, is why mechanics like friendly fire are always enabled in Helldivers 2. Yes, it makes the game more punishing, but it also helps it stand out.

Curd said that DED.NET betas and playtests have already shown evidence of a positive response to the game, and the initial spark of a fandom revolving around its characters.

“The initial nine roster of characters have relationships with each other, with the map. They have quests outside of Win the Chicken Dinner. They have allies and rivals on the roster that you would kind of learn about,” Curd explained.

“If I ping an ally or I revive a rival, you'll kind of get that in the VO and start to understand those relationships. We're talking two or three days into our last play test, we're getting fan art depicting these love triangles. And I wasn't expecting people to get it so soon. And that shows me some people are hyper engaging with the world and becoming actual fans and not product speak audience fans. Like real people that love the world. And that's been incredibly validating for myself and the team.”

Curd, who has worked on PUBG for nine-and-a-half-years as a creative director, said that DED.NET began life as a response to a task he was set by his boss of “spreading the gospel of PUBG to the non-believers.”

“We got a lot of fans,” he said. “We got a lot of people that love our thoughtful, cerebral, tactical gameplay. See a guy 500 feet away, do you take the fight? Do you get in the car? Do you retreat? But it's not for everybody. But we think the theme of PUBG, of survival of the fittest or dog eat dog or desperate survival, it's a good juicy theme. I think you could make a PUBG Match-3! And that might be what I pitch next!

“Can we find a different audience that would still engage with that vibe and engage with that world and engage with that IP? So I think, ‘Okay, so don't make more PUBG, but find more PUBG fans. Where do you begin?'

“So it sounds kind of maybe stupidly obvious, but I just made a list. It's like, what is cool shit that PUBG does well? Number one, it's an infinite story engine. One match, survival of the fittest, one winner, 99 losers. And I think it's endured for 10 years because anyone I talk to can tell me usually in high detail about their first Chicken Dinner. So that's the first thing you think. Well, what's the opposite of that? Could that infinite story engine persist over multiple matches? And so that was the first idea that's like, that sounds good and that would not work in PUBG because it breaks that promise of perfectly fair, perfectly balanced, single shot adventure.

“Could it be a multi-match journey? What does that mean? Originally our cheesy internal lingo was body persistence. And it was, if you swim, you'll get hypothermia and you'll be coughing. And if you get shot in the head, your ears will ring for a long time. And as we stood it up and tried it, we found that it changed the way that fans would play. They were not playing to win. They were playing to not get hurt. They're like, ‘This sucks. We don't like this.’ And it's like, oh, what if the injuries were more interesting and told better stories, just sneezing in the smoke or it hurts when you swim, or you occasionally fumble your weapon on weapon swap and you swear, or maybe you have a tick where you constantly spam taunts and give away your position? Or my favorite one, Stuntman, where when you slide or dive, occasionally there's an explosion behind you because it looks cool, but it might hurt you. It might frag your teammates.

“The genesis was I love hero shooters, but I never find exactly my favorite one. I always end up settling for the one I hate least. It's never the right combination of look and abilities for what I'm after. So we thought, could we challenge the player to go on a multi-match adventure where they're picking and choosing and making interesting decisions about who they want to be when they grow up, while managing these hilarious and weird injuries and racing against a clock of a diminishing career HP of you can only play so many before you're overwhelmed by injuries and you have to retire? That's the genesis of the product.”

Players can now also register for the upcoming closed beta. There’s no release window yet, but PUBG: DED.NET is due out on PC, PlayStation 5, and Xbox Series X and S.

Wesley is Director, News at IGN. Find him on Twitter at @wyp100. You can reach Wesley at wesley_yinpoole@ign.com or confidentially at wyp100@proton.me.

articles.title: Exodus Plays Exactly How a New Mass Effect Should | IGN Hands-on Preview
articles.summary: Exodus is ambitious in the same way that Mass Effect was, and now I'm expecting it to live up to that ambition.
articles.body:
Exodus’s space-opera vibes immediately reminded me of Mass Effect, and that seems to be on purpose.

Its Paladin/Immortal morality system reflects the Paragon/Renegade system, but it's going for something deeper than just good/evil and is centered around preserving humanity.

Combat feels like an evolution of Mass Effect, sharing many similartieis with shooting mechanics and controlling your allies' abilities.

When the team at Archetype Entertainment showed us the latest trailer for Exodus before the premiere at Opening Night Live, it seemed like they had understood the assignment – emotional, character-driven stories that felt natural for a space-opera RPG in the vein of Mass Effect. It was the reveal of the party member Salt, an Awakened octopus who pilots a mech to fight and protect her home. Her contentious attitude toward the player-protagonist Jun Aslan contrasts with the deep care she has for her species, and through a brief trailer, showed how it's channeling the sentiments of Interstellar; outside of Matthew McConaughey being in this, too.

But that's one piece of what a game like this needs – albeit, an incredibly important one. I played a little over an hour of Exodus and saw for myself how the gameplay piece of that puzzle comes into place. Punchy third-person shooting with two party members whose tech- and biotic-coded abilities you command through a wheel as time slows, it's like I was playing a legally distinct BioWare game. Archetype isn't shy about the parallels here nor should they be, because from my brief time with Exodus, it seems to be filling that massive void effectively .

I played an entire mission that had me and two party members infiltrating a construct in space called Khonsu, which orbits humanity's new home planet Lidon. Khonsu is also where a species of Awakened frogs, called the Kay, have established their home and maintain Lidon's defense. (For context, Awakened are hyper-intelligent animals found across Exodus' universe.) They'd been enslaved by a hostile human faction run by Gideon Aslan, Jun's half-sibling, the ruler of Lidon, and one of Exodus' main villains. It was our job to free the Kay; and maybe not entirely out of the goodness of our hearts, but in hopes of them becoming key allies, at least.

After a few cutscenes to build the mission's tension, I'm immediately thrust into combat and within seconds of touching this new game I'd never played, muscle memory kicked in as if I'd been here before. Elise, who controls a hulking mech, focuses on brute force and has attacks that can break armor, while Suliman is an agile agent who can incisively inflict heavy damage. I largely relied on calling in their abilities whenever they were ready while blasting away with my standard arsenal of rifles and shotguns, but there's a synergistic system that also paves the way for a primer-detantor type of dynamic if you can line things up.

There's a little bit of stealth if you want to get the jump on a few unsuspecting foes, and Suliman's Shadow Step can take out a standard target in one go when used undetected. But Exodus thrives on chunky combat – having Elise fire off a barrage of Knockdown Missiles or using my own ground-pound ability that shoots a line AoE and sends targets into the air, that's the good stuff. Jun has a mix of tools like an EMP grenade, homing explosive, or shield-piercing weapons that are crucial against barriers and a suite of special moves called Glyphs through his sci-fi powered Gauntlet. Even as Jun alone, you can create combos such as freezing an enemy with Petrify and following it up with an Erupt to break them. The cover system is a little iffy, especially for a game that relies pretty heavily on it, but what matters more to me is that Exodus offers the tools you'd want out of an action-RPG paired with solid, impactful gunplay.

As I made my way through Khonsu, a few standard encounters against weaker human enemies were broken up with battles against alien-esque mechanized freaks and more intimidating foes in robosuits in specific combat arenas where cover spots are clearly waist high. Some felt more like bullet sponges, although I didn't mind in the moment as it let me test the extent of the party's powers. The mission concluded with a boss fight against an Awakened bear named Captain Irina Bruin (clever), armor-clad and beastly charging at me and casting huge AoE electrical shocks. However, I was of two minds – boss fights are nice ways to stretch the limits of your combat prowess, but can feel like fitting a square peg in a round hole if the encounter isn't really designed for its gameplay systems. This fight was more about constantly dodging with a little verticality sprinkled in thanks to the battery charged pillars in the arena, and flowed like a war of attrition more than anything. Granted, this was a fairly early-game mission and I did enjoy the challenge, but my hope is that other boss fights play more into the strengths Exodus clearly exhibits.

Exodus is going to have hub areas and cities to explore, of course. But on missions like this, there are things to find off the beaten path and optional objectives along the way. Some of Jun's abilities work as exploration tools, such as Petrify being used to freeze obstructions or Erupt for clearing obstacles in the way, and you also have Shape to raise floors and a grappling hook to reach specifically marked points to reach optional areas. What's more is that you can come across unique interactions with characters you wouldn't have seen otherwise, which may lead to decisions that can come back around, sway your alignment with party members, or give a little backstory for the mission. This is in addition to finding the more tangible rewards like additional gear, crafting materials, or knowledge points to upgrade Jun's capabilities.

This is an RPG, after all, and Exodus' progression system looks to be pretty robust from what I was able to gather from looking at the menus. I had a prearranged build centered around the Soldier branch, but there were so many more directions you can spec into (Knight, Prodigy, Oracle, Operative, and Specialist, which lean into perks and buffs for different playstyles). I could see several other Gauntlet Glyphs locked at this point in the story as well, so I'm looking forward to seeing if there's an element of build crafting here because so far, combat feels like it has the sauce.

One of the optional objectives tasked me with liberating one of the Kay stuck in the test tube by defeating a wave of enemies and finding a battery to get the power back on in the room. I was rewarded with a goofy dialogue sequence, a little lore on the Kay, an approval boost from Suliman, and an upgrade for my gear. Much earlier in the mission, I had to decide the fate of a dying zealot who only just realized the wicked ways of the faction he was working for; give him a health pack and hope he changes his ways in the future or let him die out. I didn't see the result of this in the demo, but when it comes to choice and consequence in Exodus, the most indicative moment was in the decision you have to make at the end of this mission.

See, Suliman is an operative of the Tenjin Dynasty, and he would prefer to have the Kay under their direct influence after liberating them. When Suliman proposes altering the Kay's communication beacons to guarantee full loyalty across generations, you can either push back or go along with this plan. I pushed back, questioning the idea of manipulating them after restoring their independence, to which Suliman simply says, "The irony is not lost on me." "That's all you have to say?" Jun replies. Jun implies he was misled and that this is what Gideon would've wanted. They go back and forth about how loyalty ensures protection and the Kay leader you saved isn't entirely opposed to it. And so you're left with a simple choice: make the alteration or leave the beacons alone. What good is security if you give up freedom, right? I leave the beacons alone, promising to protect Khonsu as a matter of principle and Jun concludes, "You don't get to call the shots for sentient beings and claim it's for their own good." Suliman abides by the decision, and is surprisingly supportive in the end.

It's a bit textbook in the choice-based RPG playbook, and the dialogue tees this up quite predictably. But I think what's important here is how it's contextualized for the broader story and in the writing itself. This particular scene gives me hope that Exodus knows how to frame these big moments in their delivery and the in-game impact (hinted in the visual bubble next to the choice showing Jun's predictive powers), even if they sometimes boil down to a binary choice. This is also the first big moment where I saw Exodus' version of the Paragon/Renegade morality system – here, it's denoted as Paladin/Immortal. Narrative director Drew Karpyshyn (who you may know as a renowned narrative designer on Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic and Mass Effect) described this system as more of a push-and-pull between preserving your humanity versus embracing the cold and calculated ways of Celestials, a transhumanist sect that plays a big role in the story, rather than simple good or evil. It may look and function similarly (shown as blue and red choices, respectively), but I expect the system to grow more nuanced as the story goes on and more decisions compile into varying consequences that are reflected in the Jun you'll shape.

Exodus has a clear goofy edge to it, especially with the Kay being silly frogs with names derived from the number and section of the ship they were born in. Early in the mission, you meet 42C, who's listening to loud rock music and greets you with an irreverent attitude that contrasts with the serious tone of the initial infiltration cutscene. I am wary of characters being too quippy, like Elise, who keeps commenting on every little thing happening in battle or how things kinda lean into the cheesy sense of humor you'd see on a CW show. I'm not entirely put off by that, I just hope it knows when to reign it in and strike the right balance for a story that seems to wield the gravity of humanity's survival in space.

The consequences of the decisions you make will be exacerbated by the fact that Exodus's story abides by the scientific theories of relativity and time dilation. We'll see characters affected in different ways by the passage of time – and going back to the trailer I mentioned at the beginning, it feels like Archetype knows the material it's working with in order to win the hearts and minds of those who are looking for that emotional space opera adventure. From my conversation with Drew Karpyshyn , I get the impression that even with a little levity to take the edge off, there's a greater emphasis on trying to deliver on impactful storytelling. The inclusion of romance options regardless of gender, being able to play as a male or female Jun, and having a relationship system all folded into your alignments as time warps in a journey to find humanity's new home – Exodus is ambitious in the same way that Mass Effect was, and now I'm expecting it to live up to that ambition.

While you're here, check out these recent previews of other big upcoming games we've checked out recently!

Michael Higham is an editor at IGN who regularly contributes with reviews, previews, features, and news in written and video form. He's usually entrusted with covering long RPGs and tech products, but he's got range when it comes to games. You'll also catch him at events and hosting video content, including IGN's weekly podcast Unlocked .

articles.title: Exodus Narrative Director Explains Romance, Relationships, and Mass Effect Comparisons in New Sci-Fi RPG
articles.summary: The upcoming space opera RPG Exodus has drawn a lot Mass Effect comparisons, and its narrative director worked on both. He explains their differences and more.
articles.body:
Your first impression of Exodus was probably, "Oh, this looks like Mass Effect." And narrative director Drew Karpyshyn, who was a narrative lead on BioWare's legendary space opera RPG series, told me, "It's a perfectly fine way to wrap your head around it." He'd love for Exodus to be regarded in the same way, and it's easy to see why. Exodus has all the pieces you'd want from a spiritual successor sci-fi RPG: tough decisions to make about the fate of humanity in space, punchy action combat, and the tangled web of character relationships you influence.

After playing Exodus myself, I talked with Karpyshyn about building out a new universe with developer Archetype Entertainment and many of the philosophies driving its RPG elements. How does the morality system work? How do you romance the characters you adore? And why should players care about the choices they make and how are they reflected in a story that needs to feel impactful? We dig into all that and more.

Parts of our discussion reference the demo I played, so be sure to read my Exodus hands-on preview for additional context about the story and gameplay elements we touch on, or you can watch the video version below.

IGN: The thing that jumps out to me and I'm most curious about is how you're handling choice and consequence. In the demo, I saw the Paladin-Immortal alignment system, kind of reflective of the Paragon-Renegade in Mass Effect. I want to dig more into the morality system, how it works and how you're thinking of choice and consequence in the context of that.

Drew Karpyshyn: Those are all related, for sure, but I'll start with choice and consequence. Obviously, we think choice is very important in our RPG and we want it to matter. So, we want it to have an impact on the story; how decisions you make impact the direction the story goes. We want it to impact your companions, your relationships and how they feel about you, and the romances. And we want it to affect things in gameplay and have choices matter there.

We look at it as if there are three levels of choices. There's the small moment to moment choices, like what do I say in a particular dialogue; maybe it's something small that has characters saying something different, and you can get little funny moments. We have more mid-level choices, which are things like building affinity with a companion, maybe going down one of the morality paths, maybe doing something with a character who's going to show up later. And then we have our sort of "gold-level" choices, which are like these big consequential moments in the story.

You got a glimpse of one of them at the end of the Khonsu mission [from the preview demo]. There was what we call the breakpoint. There's a decision you make at the end about what to do with the Kay's beacons. You have a couple of options, whether you side with Suliman [or leave the beacons alone]. And breakpoints are where Jun has these predictive abilities. Not so much prophetic, more like if you've read The Foundation [book series by Isaac Asimov] with hyper-accurate prediction models. This gives you insight on what direction decisions will go and what the potential consequences are. What you saw in the demo is pretty early in Jun's development, so as you get further in the game, you can develop those abilities and get more information about what the long-term consequences of those choices will be. So, we want to have those choices affect the world you're in, the future of your society, your companions, your friends, your choices in gameplay, and so on. To us, choice is incredibly important and that's sort of our overall philosophy.

I'll jump into the Paladin-Immortal side of things. That's our morality spectrum. It's a little bit different than simple good or evil. There are elements of that, but a huge part of our game revolves around Jun as a human who has certain genetic upgrades or anomalies that allow you to interact with Celestial technology, and you kind of bridge the gap between humans and Celestials. One of the key things here is: how do you want to grow and evolve? And the Paladin path is where Jun decides to hold onto their humanity, maybe rejecting some of the darker elements of the Celestials. And maybe you don't want to mess with it because it could have dangerous consequences, it could change you in certain ways. The Immortal path is more for the sake of strength and power, and to survive, you embrace some of the darker elements of the Celestials. In general, Celestials are typically seen to be less empathetic, less compassionate, and a little more ruthless.

We kind of have you walking down these paths and often it's tied into choices you make, and again, whether or not you embrace Celestial technology, Celestial upgrades, things like that. Or whether you want to try to hold onto your humanity even if it means you're working at a bit of a disadvantage but don't want to lose the core of what you are.

IGN: I've talked to folks like Leonard Boyarsky and Todd Howard about how they incorporate choice and consequence in their games and how they think of friction. When you make a choice and it locks you out of certain things or it might make something harder, you're making huge games and want players to see everything, but at a certain point when you have a game like this, there are paths you have to take that give players a sense of meaningful agency. Are those things you consider, and how do you approach that?

Karpyshyn: I mean, that's a very good point. The key to choices are consequences, and consequences have to have a cost. So, one of those costs is when you go down certain paths, you close off other paths. There's going to be content in the game you will not see on one playthrough. That's the way it is with the way the game is designed. We have a lot of optional content as well, but even within that optional content, there are choices that will lock or unlock certain things, change the way things play out, change relationships, change characters, change… future… missions…

Uh yeah, I gotta be careful, I can't say too much, I don't want to spoil too much! I mean, that's a huge part of this game. We want to put pressure on the player. We want them to be a little bit conflicted. We want them to think, 'Oh, I know I'm giving something up when I make this choice, but I'm also gaining something.' So again,, I think that's a huge part of choice in games, is that you have to have some cost and consequence.

IGN: How do you approach character relationships? You alluded to relationship dynamics between party members and I'm assuming other key characters. I want to dig into that a little bit more with how they work in Exodus and how you've thought about structuring them.

Karpyshyn: So, you'll have a number of allies with you. Some of them are combat companions that come with you on missions, you can select them as party members. Others are very important characters who don't come with you on missions, but serve other roles within the game. And each of those companions has their own hopes, dreams, desires, wants, goals, needs. They're not always on the same page as you and often in conflict with you, but they're often in conflict with each other as well. So, you have to sort of navigate who you want to make happy and who you'll have to disappoint.

This ties in with romances as well. Again, we want to put you in positions where you can't make everybody happy. You're going to have to choose. Who do you side with, knowing that you will gain or lose affinity with one of these companions? It will change their relationship. You could be in a position where you really like a particular companion, but in a specific situation, you really disagree with what they want. So, as a player, which do you value more? Do you value the outcome of this decision or do you value the relationship with this companion? And you have to juggle it. That's a decision you make as a player.

A huge part of that is making companions feel real, making their relationship with you grow, allowing it to sort of evolve from the choices you've made and realizing that the choices you make are going to bring some companions closer to you, but maybe push some companions farther away. And again, without spoiling too much, we definitely want to have it impact how their storylines go. And depending on choices you make, by the end of the game, you might not have every companion with you that you started with. That's about all I can say!

IGN: Something that's always brewing in conversations is how games portray romance. You want them to feel organic, whereas some might see them as more like a mechanical aspect of a game. Between having something that feels natural and human-like or something that focuses on feeding into gameplay systems, how are you thinking about romance in particular when it comes to Exodus?

Karpyshyn: Of course, it's a spectrum. But for us, we're leaning more toward the romances being a sort of role-playing relationship thing as opposed to being tied directly to gameplay. First of all, the player drives the romances and they are not gender-locked. But there's no situation where a character is going to romance you if you didn't take the initiative. We want to put you in situations where you can potentially try to romance more than one character. Sometimes it'll go well, sometimes it won't depending on the character and depending on the choices you make. Like real life, it's complicated, right? We want it to be complicated. We want players to get in situations where they're struggling to get what they want out of a relationship.

We generally want that to be something that affects your relationship with that companion. Now with that companion, as I said, these things can affect what happens to them later in the game. But it's not something where we're tying it directly into gameplay, like romance giving you a boost to your skills or something like that. There are systems for that, but we keep them separate from each other.

IGN: So, you advance these through dialogue options, but also through choices you make throughout the story?

Karpyshyn: Yeah, it's a combination of dialogue options and there's a lot of side content for each companion that you can do optionally, or maybe cannot do. Of course, the more time you spend with the companion, the more that you have a chance to deepen that relationship. Or rather, emphasize that relationship; if you're on bad terms with someone and you keep doing missions with them and keep making choices they hate, it'll get worse, right? But you also have a chance to push it in another direction if you want and bounce back.

IGN: You can choose to play as a male or female Jun, but are there any specific differences? Maybe not in the main story or gameplay but in how certain dialogue is written or how the characters react to you. Does any of that change?

Karpyshyn: We really want players to feel like their choice of whether to play male or female is the choice that makes them happy. We didn't focus a lot on trying to make the story be particularly different or unique based on that specific choice. We want you to feel like you can inhabit Jun, and then we're telling a story that works regardless of which choice you make. So, there's not a lot of differences in how characters react to you based on that. It's more based on what choices you make in the moment, what choices you make relating to them or your interactions with them that will change how they react to you.

IGN: I'm curious about how time dilation plays into the story and how it works. You had mentioned it factoring into choices you make – is that tied to story progression or is it housed in specific decisions you make throughout?

Karpyshyn: In the universe of Exodus, time dilation is a huge thing. They have to deal with it, it's something that fundamentally shapes how their societies and worlds are formed and built and how they interact with each other. Because going on an exodus, going on a journey to another system, is going to take years and years even though for you it will only seem like it's maybe taking a few days because of time dilation, years are going to pass back home – maybe decades, maybe centuries. So, it's a very big deal. It's a major life event. It's not something you do over and over and over again.

You have to make sure you're properly prepared before you go. A lot of your focus is on making sure you have the right allies, the right team, and everything's in place before you go on this exodus to make sure that when you come back, things will have gone in the direction you wanted. We talked a little bit about the traveler dynasties. These are the organizations you set up to make sure things stay on track while you're gone; trusted people who hopefully deal with problems as they come up and push things in the direction you want.

So, when you go on an exodus in Exodus, when you go on these journeys, it's a major narrative event. It's a major life event. When you come back, there will have been major consequences that have happened. But we want to make it clear that these are things that you build up to and that you prepare for before going on these very important and dangerous exodus missions. When you come back, then you must deal with the consequences.

A lot of it is about what you do before and what you do after that impacts these narrative events. As I said, the exodus itself is a major life event, they aren't something that you're going on every week! Not every mission is an exodus mission – for example, Khonsu, the one you played just now is a space station orbiting your homeworld, so there's no time dilation in that particular mission. But other missions when you go outside your system then come back, you will see the consequences of time dilation. Yes, it's very deliberate and clear what you're doing [in these scenarios].

IGN: The political structures are such a strong part of worldbuilding in a lot of sci-fi. Mass Effect with the Systems Alliance or Star Trek with the Federation and Klingon – all these worlds are held up by their political fiction. What can you share in terms of how Exodus incorporates that?

Karpyshyn: I don't know if you've read the Peter Hamilton books, but every corner of the Exodus universe, every part of the cluster is going to have their own systems and they'll develop very independently because, again, you're separated by light years, by time and space. So on Lidon [the human homeworld] and in many of the human worlds, the traveler dynasties are a huge part of this political system because they are the ones who drive the progress of humanity by finding the technology and dealing with existential threats. And because they're the ones making these sacrifices and taking these risks, they want to make sure there are structures in place to preserve what they're fighting for when they get back. They don't want to come back and find everything they cared about is gone. So, the traveler dynasties are a huge part of Exodus and a huge part of Lidon.

Jun's father, Orion Aslan, was the leader of a very powerful traveler dynasty [the Aslan Dynasty] and went missing, and your half-sibling [Gideon Aslan, a major villain] basically takes over and you have to go into hiding. So, a large part of the game is about reclaiming this heritage, reclaiming control of your dynasty and then choosing how your dynasty is going to work, forming alliances with other dynasties like the Tenjin Dynasty, which Suliman belongs to. Khonsu is the first mission with him and it's sort of like your first step in forging your alliances with his dynasty. Those political systems are important and they're a key to helping shape and control the future of your homeworld of Lidon.

IGN: You have a game where you make choices and they have these grand statements about humanity. What do you want the player to come out of Exodus with in terms of messages or just things that they are going to stew on when they finish this game?

Karpyshyn: One of the things we're thinking a lot about is underlying themes. We have many themes in Exodus and a big one for us is evolution, growth, and change. The Celestials evolved from humans, they became something very, very different. The awakened evolved from normal animals on Earth. How do those changes in growth and evolution differ?

Another key theme we like to explore is sacrifice. The travelers have to make these immense sacrifices. When you go on these missions to save your world, by the time you come back, the world may have moved on. Things may be very different. The thing you are actually trying to save might not even exist anymore. Knowing you'll be gone for years or decades and leaving behind the people you love, the people you care about, leaving your home behind, it's a huge cost and a huge sacrifice. And that's something that we really want to explore. What sacrifices are you willing to make? What price are you willing to pay to get what you want? And then what happens when it doesn't quite work out the way you want? How do you feel about that sacrifice? And even when you're making it, knowing that it might not even work the way you want.

I'd say those for me are the two big themes we like to explore, and we just want players to get the sense when they play the game that we've given them a chance to explore these themes in a way they really enjoy. Maybe we've made them think about these things a little bit differently, put them into situations where they've really had to struggle with this internal conflict and put that burden on them. Sounds bad to put a burden on our players! But we do, we want to put the burden of choice on them and make them struggle.

IGN: That's what makes these games compelling and memorable, right? Tough decisions. I really enjoy that part of these kinds of games… like in Mass Effect! I know you're always getting those comparisons, but I'm interested in how you feel about those comparisons and how has that feeling changed as time has gone on?

Karpyshyn: Having worked on Mass Effect, people are making comparisons. The same thing happened when we were doing Mass Effect where people were making comparisons to Knights of the Old Republic, which I also worked on! You're always going to get comparisons to things you've worked on before and the team has worked on before. And I actually don't mind that because I feel like the core of what we do is not in the details of something rather it's the spirit of what we've done. The spirit of the type of games that I love to make, the games I love to play, is something I try to capture with every game. We always want to put a fresh spin on it.

But I'll be honest, if five years from now, people are putting us up in that same pantheon with those other projects I've worked on in the past, I would love that! I mean, that's great! We look at Exodus and we have a lot of different inspirations. Same thing with other projects I've worked on. There are always dozens and dozens of inspirations, you take little bits and pieces, and you weave them together into something you hope is fresh and new. You try to put a spin on it that players haven't had before, and you try to just give them something that they can understand at a core level that can evoke a lot of the emotions they're hoping for, but then also give them something that surprises them, delights them, catches them off guard.

I think it's a perfectly fine way for people to wrap their heads around things and I always love it when people say they love past things I've done. And I think people are going to really, really like what we're doing for Exodus because we've just captured the spirit and energy of the of the games we've worked on in the past, and we've brought them in to our new project, and we're very excited to let people finally finally experience it soon.

IGN: Of course, you've worked on so many games and you've influenced the direction of RPGs; I remember being 12 years old thinking Knights of the Old Republic was the coolest thing in the world, and it still is to this day. Good RPGs age well. But in those decades since, how have you felt about the evolution and direction of RPGs as a whole? What speaks to you that you've seen other people work on? Do you think there's something missing in the genre?

Karpyshyn: For me, the cool thing is seeing the evolution as technology gets better and seeing what developers do with that. And then also seeing developers just build on everything that came before. Obviously, there are a lot of amazing RPGs that have come out in the last few years. Baldur's Gate 3 is amazing, Expedition 33 is amazing. There's just a lot of amazing stuff going on in role-playing, narrative, and storytelling. The industry continues to mature, evolve, and advance, and for me, basically seeing everybody inspiring and pushing each other; you know, seeing somebody do something amazing pushes you and challenges you, too. You see how the bar's been raised and that bar keeps getting raised. Seeing that slow evolution over my time in the industry is very exciting.

It's always challenging and makes it harder to come up with the next evolution, but I think that's what makes it fun, is you have to find new ways to challenge yourself to up the ante, to raise that bar one more time. I don't know if I would say anything's missing in the industry because new stuff keeps coming. I'm always interested to see whatever new RPG comes out, look at what they've done, what they've experimented with, and how I can then think about those things and incorporate them into the projects that I want to work on and that I care about.

Michael Higham is an editor at IGN who regularly contributes with reviews, previews, features, and news in written and video form. He's usually entrusted with covering long RPGs and tech products, but he's got range when it comes to games. You'll also catch him at events and hosting video content, including IGN's weekly podcast Unlocked .

articles.title: How Explicit Are the Sex Scenes in Exodus? It Sounds Like Mass Effect Fans Will Find Them Familiar
articles.summary: How explicit are the sex scenes in Mass Effect-style game, Exodus? We asked the developers.
articles.body:
As a big fan of Mass Effect and its various romanceable companions, I wanted to put the record straight on the ins and outs of Exodus’ sex scenes. After all, Exodus looks and feels a lot like Mass Effect. It’s even developed by some of the brains behind BioWare’s much-loved sci-fi RPG franchise. So, it feels reasonable to me to compare and contrast what goes on under the sheets in both games.

At gamescom, I interviewed game director Chris King, narrative director Drew Karpyshyn, and general manager Chad Robertson, about all things Exodus, and thought the part of our chat about the sex scenes would be worth closer inspection. I began by asking what to me felt like the most obvious starting point: can you have sex with the octopus?

What octopus? Exodus has a number of companions, some of which are non-human. As an 'Awakened' octopus, Salt pilots a specialized combat mech, and can eject ink-like smokescreens that confuse and disorient enemies. She exists in a tank that keeps her alive out on the battlefield.

The answer, perhaps unfortunately for some, is no, you can’t have sex with Salt. “Sadly no romance with Salt,” Karpyshyn confirmed. “And that's mostly because Salt just thinks humans are gross. We’ve only got four limbs. She’s like, that’s weird!”

While Exodus won’t let you have sex with Salt, it does feature lots of romance options, and the game does not block them by gender. Romance is something the player will have to actively pursue, which means you won’t accidentally fall into a romance. Romance can also cause conflict between companions, depending on the choices you make. “You're not going to be able to keep everybody happy,” Karpyshyn said. “You're not going to be able to get everyone to go and change the way you want to. Just like real life, we want it to be messy and complicated.”

But how mature is Exodus? As an M-rated game, some might have thought Exodus' sex scenes would be explicit. But they're “very tastefully done,” Karpyshyn teased. “We allow you to get physical, but they're tastefully done,” King added.

“Across the industry there's different bars that are set, and I would say we're somewhere in the appropriate middle,” Karpyshyn said.

What is that appropriate middle, exactly? Baldur’s Gate 3, for example, features nudity in its sex scenes (you can even have sex with The Emperor, who’s a sort of octopus-like humanoid). CD Projekt’s Cyberpunk 2077, meanwhile, holds nothing back. The sex scenes in Mass Effect though, are brief and never explicit — despite what Fox News would have you think.

It sounds like Exodus’ sex scenes are along the same lines as Mass Effect’s. “I think we're a bit closer to the reserved side, but certainly it's clear what's happening, but tasteful is a good way to describe it,” King explained.

So, you can't have sex with Salt the Octopus. That much we do know. So who can you have sex with? Exodus companions include Elise Charroux, a "blunt, no-nonsense ‘Sleeper’ from 23rd-century Earth," Kara Voss, a pilot and mechanic "known for precision flying and confident attitude," and Suliman, the "wealthy, reclusive, and dangerous" operative. All three, I think, will be popular romance options.

In addition to Salt the Octopus being off limits, I doubt Exodus will let you have sex with Houston, an Awakened wolf who was orphaned at a young age and raised alongside main character Jun as an adopted brother. Houston is described as a "story companion," but romancing a talking wolf who's "always watching over his human sibling" would be weird on a lot of levels.

Exodus launches on PC, PlayStation 5, and Xbox Series X and S on April 7, 2027.

Wesley is Director, News at IGN. Find him on Twitter at @wyp100. You can reach Wesley at wesley_yinpoole@ign.com or confidentially at wyp100@proton.me.

articles.title: Nintendo Confirms 2 Nintendo Direct Broadcasts for Next Week, Including a Dedicated Legend of Zelda 40th Anniversary Broadcast
articles.summary: Nintendo has announced a pair of Nintendo Direct broadcasts for next week, including a dedicated Legend of Zelda 40th Anniversary showcase.
articles.body:
Nintendo has announced a pair of Nintendo Direct broadcasts for next week, including a dedicated Legend of Zelda 40th Anniversary showcase.

The Zelda Direct will air on Tuesday, September 8 at 7am Pacific / 10am Eastern / 3pm UK time, and last 30 minutes. Expect updates on the Zelda franchise, including this year's Ocarina of Time remake, and perhaps a first proper look at next year's live-action Legend of Zelda movie.

Nintendo's next general Direct will then air 24 hours later, on Wednesday, September 9 at 7am Pacific / 10am Eastern / 3pm UK time, and last 45 minutes. This will then be followed by a 110-minute Nintendo Treehouse stream, with further gameplay of titles featured in the Direct.

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time Trailer June 2026 Nintendo Direct - Screenshots

I strongly expect Nintendo to show off its Ocarina of Time remake in detail, and give fans more of a sense of how the company has updated its N64 classic. Remember, of course, that Nintendo has confirmed it will launch its Ocarina remake this year — and there's not that much of 2026 left.

With Nintendo keeping to a monthly launch cadence of Switch 2 games so far this year, and Switch Sports Resort already dropping in October, will Zelda launch opposite GTA 6 in November? There's not long now for us to find out.

What else could we see here? With time also ticking down until Nintendo and Sony's live-action Zelda movie, now seems the right time to make the rest of the film's casting official — although much of it has now leaked. Officially, Nintendo has only confirmed Benjamin Evan Ainsworth and Bo Bragason as Link and Zelda, though it's been widely reported that Uli Latukefu will play Ganondorf and Dichen Lachman will play Impa, while Yvonne Strahovski, Lydia Peckham and the late Sam Neil are also part of the cast . I'm expecting a teaser trailer to drop, too.

Finally, keep an eye out for those fancy Legend of Zelda 40th Anniversary Switch 2 consoles and Joy-Con . Here's hoping they don't cost too many rupees.

Moving onto the main Direct, what might we see here? Upcoming Switch 2 games such as Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave (launching September 17) and Nintendo Switch Sports Resort (October 22) are safe bets. Beyond those, and Ocarina, Nintendo has not said much of its 2027 slate. Could we get a glimpse of the company's long-awaited 3D Mario? It'd be lovely to think so, but this is far from assured. Still, I'm expecting to see at least one more Switch 2 title added to its release list for early next year from a smaller Nintendo series, perhaps a new Luigi's Mansion or 2D Metroid.

As ever, IGN will be reporting on all of the big announcements as they happen — be sure to watch with us next week.
